passage_text: Giant axons were voltage-clamped and their action potentials recorded at 20 °C in artificial seawater. Peak depolarization and conduction velocity were measured before and after adding channel blockers or changing extracellular potassium. Table 1 reports the resting potential, the peak of the action potential and the conduction velocity. Tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, and lidocaine is a use-dependent sodium channel blocker.
table_data:

|---|---|---|---|
| Control | -70 | +35 | 50 |
| TTX 1 µM | -70 | -68 | 0 |
| Lidocaine 0.5 mM | -70 | +5 | 8 |
| High potassium, 10 mM | -55 | +20 | 25 |
| TEA 10 mM | -70 | +45 | 20 |
| Ouabain 1 µM | -68 | +30 | 40 |
stem: Why does the resting potential sit near -70 mV rather than at the sodium equilibrium potential?

options.A: Voltage-gated sodium channels are open at rest
options.B: The sodium-potassium pump sets the potential directly
options.C: Chloride is the only permeant ion at rest
options.D: The membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to sodium at rest

explanation: At rest, potassium leak channels dominate the membrane conductance, so the membrane potential sits near the potassium equilibrium potential of about -90 mV, pulled slightly positive by a small sodium leak. The pump contributes a few millivolts because it is electrogenic, but permeability sets the resting value. Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest.
memorize: Resting potential is set mainly by potassium permeability
The Na/K pump is electrogenic but contributes only a few mV

fm.formula: Vm is a permeability-weighted average of equilibrium potentials
fm.variables: Potassium conductance dominates at rest; sodium conductance is small
fm.values: potassium equilibrium about -90 mV, sodium equilibrium about +60 mV
fm.substitution: not needed; weighting is qualitative at rest
fm.why: The Goldman equation weights each ion's equilibrium potential by its permeability, and potassium permeability is much larger at rest
fm.no_calc: Higher permeability to potassium pulls Vm toward -90

correct_rationale_plain: Potassium leak conductance dominates at rest, so the membrane potential stays near the potassium equilibrium potential.

wrong.B: The pump maintains gradients and adds a small electrogenic component, but it does not set the potential directly
wrong.C: Chloride contributes, but potassium permeability is the main determinant
wrong.A: Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest; opening them causes the upstroke

stem: TTX abolishes the action potential without changing the resting potential. What does this show?

options.B: The action potential upstroke requires voltage-gated sodium channels, while the resting potential does not
options.D: The resting potential requires voltage-gated sodium channels

explanation: TTX binds the outer pore of voltage-gated sodium channels and prevents the regenerative sodium influx that produces the upstroke. Resting potential is maintained by potassium leak channels and the pump, so it is unaffected. This separation is why TTX can silence action potentials without depolarizing the cell.
memorize: TTX blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
Action potential upstroke is sodium-dependent; resting potential is potassium-dependent

fm.formula: upstroke rate depends on sodium conductance
fm.variables: TTX reduces sodium conductance to near zero
fm.values: peak falls from +35 to -68 mV, resting stays at -70 mV
fm.why: Without sodium entry the membrane cannot depolarize past threshold, so no regenerative spike occurs
fm.no_calc: No spike but normal rest means the blocked channel is specific to the upstroke

correct_rationale_plain: TTX blocks the sodium channels that carry the upstroke, leaving the potassium-based resting potential intact.

wrong.A: Potassium channel block is TEA, which broadens the spike instead of abolishing it
wrong.C: TTX binds the channel pore and does not alter ion gradients
wrong.D: Resting potential persists without voltage-gated sodium channels

sc: TTX kills the spike, not the rest.

stem: Lidocaine lowers the peak to +5 mV and slows conduction to 8 m/s. What property of local anesthetics does this illustrate?

options.B: They block sodium channels preferentially in rapidly firing tissue

explanation: Lidocaine binds the inner pore of voltage-gated sodium channels, and its binding is favored when channels are open or inactivated, so rapidly firing neurons accumulate more block. That use dependence explains why local anesthetics silence pain fibers without stopping every neuron equally. The peak falls because fewer sodium channels are available for the upstroke.
memorize: Local anesthetics are use-dependent sodium channel blockers
More frequent firing means more drug binding and more block

fm.formula: block increases with the fraction of channels in the open or inactivated state
fm.variables: Use dependence arises because the drug accesses the pore only when the channel opens
fm.values: peak +35 to +5 mV, velocity 50 to 8 m/s
fm.why: Repeated opening gives repeated access to the binding site, so high-frequency tissue accumulates block
fm.no_calc: Lower peak with slower conduction means fewer active sodium channels

correct_rationale_plain: Lidocaine blocks sodium channels in a use-dependent way, so rapidly firing pain fibers are silenced first.

wrong.A: Potassium channel activation would speed repolarization, not reduce the peak
wrong.C: Local anesthetics partition into membranes but do not dissolve them at clinical doses
wrong.D: They do not change the sodium gradient; they block the channel

sc: Use-dependent block equals more firing, more block.

stem: Raising extracellular potassium to 10 mM depolarizes the resting potential to -55 mV and reduces the peak. Why does the peak fall?

options.D: More sodium channels are inactivated at the depolarized resting potential

explanation: A less negative resting potential holds a larger fraction of voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state, so fewer are available to open on stimulation. Hyperkalemia reduces excitability despite depolarization

fm.formula: fraction of available sodium channels falls as resting potential depolarizes
fm.variables: Inactivation gates close at potentials positive to about -60 mV
fm.why: Steady depolarization shifts channels into the inactivated state, removing them from the pool that can open
fm.no_calc: Less negative rest means fewer channels ready to fire

correct_rationale_plain: Depolarizing the resting potential inactivates sodium channels, so fewer are available for the upstroke.

wrong.B: The upstroke is carried by sodium, not potassium
wrong.C: The sodium gradient is unchanged by extracellular potassium
wrong.A: Potassium channels do not close completely at -55 mV

sc: Depolarized rest equals inactivated sodium channels.

stem: TEA raises the peak to +45 mV and slows conduction. What is the mechanism?

options.B: TEA blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, delaying repolarization and broadening the spike

explanation: TEA blocks the pore of voltage-gated potassium channels from the inside, slowing the outward potassium current that repolarizes the membrane. Blocking potassium channels broadens the action potential

fm.variables: TEA reduces the delayed rectifier potassium current
fm.values: peak rises from +35 to +45 mV, velocity falls from 50 to 20 m/s
fm.why: Less outward current means the membrane takes longer to return toward rest, prolonging the spike
fm.no_calc: Broader spike means slower potassium exit

wrong.C: TEA blocks rather than opens potassium channels
wrong.D: TEA does not change ion gradients

sc: TEA equals potassium block equals wide spike.

stem: Ouabain slowly depolarizes the axon and eventually abolishes the action potential. Why?

options.B: It inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase, so ion gradients run down over time

explanation: Ouabain inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase, so sodium slowly accumulates inside and potassium is lost. fm.why: Without active transport, passive leaks gradually equalize ion concentrations across the membrane
fm.no_calc: Slow depolarization plus fading spike means gradient loss

wrong.C: Potassium channel opening would hyperpolarize rather than slowly depolarize

stem: Why do myelinated axons conduct faster than unmyelinated axons of the same diameter?

options.A: Myelin increases membrane capacitance and slows ion flow
options.C: Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier, where channels are concentrated
options.D: Myelinated axons have a higher intracellular potassium concentration

explanation: Myelin insulates the internodal membrane, so the local current spreads passively to the next node, where voltage-gated sodium channels are clustered. Regeneration occurs only at nodes, which makes conduction saltatory and much faster. Myelin lowers capacitance and raises resistance, both of which speed passive spread.
memorize: Saltatory conduction jumps node to node
Myelin lowers capacitance and raises membrane resistance

fm.formula: conduction velocity rises with membrane resistance and falls with capacitance
fm.variables: Myelin adds layers that increase resistance and decrease capacitance
fm.values: not needed; the structural effect is qualitative
fm.why: A thicker insulator lets current spread farther before leaking out, so the next node is reached sooner
fm.no_calc: Insulation plus node clustering equals fast saltatory conduction

correct_rationale_plain: Myelin insulates internodes so current spreads to the next node, where channels regenerate the spike.

wrong.A: Myelin decreases capacitance, and lower capacitance speeds conduction
wrong.B: Myelin is a lipid sheath without channels; channels sit at nodes
wrong.D: Myelin does not change intracellular ion concentrations

stem: What limits the maximum firing frequency of a neuron?

options.D: The absolute refractory period, when sodium channels are inactivated

explanation: After an action potential, voltage-gated sodium channels remain inactivated until the membrane repolarizes, which defines the absolute refractory period. No stimulus can trigger another spike during that window, so it caps the firing rate. The relative refractory period follows, when a stronger stimulus can fire the cell.
memorize: Absolute refractory period: sodium channels inactivated, no new spike possible
Refractory period sets the maximum firing frequency

fm.formula: maximum firing rate is approximately 1/refractory period
fm.variables: Refractory period is the time sodium channels remain inactivated
fm.values: a 2 ms refractory period allows at most 500 spikes per second
fm.why: Without available sodium channels the upstroke cannot be regenerated, so the interval sets a hard limit
fm.no_calc: Shorter refractory period means higher maximum rate

correct_rationale_plain: Sodium channel inactivation during the absolute refractory period prevents a second spike, capping firing frequency.

wrong.B: Glucose supply affects metabolism, not the millisecond refractory limit
wrong.C: Dendrite number affects input integration, not the spike limit
wrong.A: Resting potassium conductance affects resting potential and excitability, not the refractory ceiling directly

stem: A stimulus just below threshold produces a small depolarization that fades. Why does it not trigger an action potential?

options.A: Too few sodium channels open to produce a net inward current that exceeds the outward leak

explanation: A subthreshold stimulus opens some sodium channels, but the resulting inward current is smaller than the outward potassium leak, so the membrane repolarizes passively. At threshold, sodium entry exceeds the leak and the regenerative cycle becomes self-sustaining. This is why action potentials are all-or-none rather than graded.
memorize: Threshold is where sodium inward current exceeds potassium outward current
Action potentials are all-or-none once threshold is crossed

fm.formula: threshold is reached when inward sodium current exceeds outward leak current
fm.variables: Small depolarizations open few channels; larger ones open enough to regenerate
fm.values: not needed; the criterion is current balance
fm.why: The positive feedback of sodium channel opening only wins once recruitment is large enough to overwhelm the leak
fm.no_calc: Below threshold the leak wins, above threshold sodium wins

correct_rationale_plain: A subthreshold stimulus opens too few sodium channels, so the potassium leak repolarizes the membrane before regeneration begins.

wrong.B: Potassium channels are open, not blocked, and they are what terminates the response
wrong.C: The sodium gradient does not reverse during a subthreshold stimulus
wrong.D: Myelination affects speed, not the threshold principle

sc: Threshold equals sodium current beats leak.
mn: Not enough sodium to start the fire.

stem: How does a neuron encode stimulus intensity if every action potential has the same amplitude?

options.A: By varying the amplitude of each spike
options.C: By the frequency of action potentials and the number of active neurons
options.D: By reversing the direction of the spike

explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none, so intensity is encoded by firing rate and by recruitment of more neurons, not by spike height. Stronger stimuli produce more frequent spikes and activate more fibers. This frequency code is decoded at synapses, where repeated release accumulates transmitter.
memorize: Action potential amplitude is all-or-none
Intensity is coded by frequency and recruitment

fm.formula: intensity code = firing rate x recruited units
fm.variables: Spike amplitude is fixed; rate and population size vary
fm.values: not needed; the code is frequency-based
fm.why: Because each spike is identical, only the number of spikes per unit time can carry graded information
fm.no_calc: Same size spikes mean count them, do not measure them

correct_rationale_plain: Since spikes are all-or-none, intensity is signaled by how often they fire and how many neurons are active.

wrong.A: Amplitude is all-or-none in a given neuron
wrong.B: Resting potential is not the coding variable for intensity
wrong.D: Spike direction is fixed by channel distribution and does not encode intensity

stem: Why does the action potential propagate in one direction along an axon?

options.A: Sodium channels behind the spike are inactivated, so the wave cannot travel backward
options.B: Potassium channels are absent behind the spike
options.C: The axon membrane is polarized in only one direction

explanation: Channels immediately behind the advancing spike are refractory because their inactivation gates have not yet reset. Current can therefore depolarize only the region ahead, which is still excitable, so the wave moves forward. This refractory tail enforces one-way propagation.
memorize: Refractory tail behind the spike enforces one-way propagation
Inactivated sodium channels cannot be re-excited immediately

fm.formula: propagation direction is set by which neighboring region is excitable
fm.variables: Ahead of the spike channels are closed but available; behind they are inactivated
fm.values: not needed; the mechanism is refractory state
fm.why: Current spreads in both directions, but only the region with available channels can regenerate a spike
fm.no_calc: Behind is refractory, ahead is ready, so the spike moves forward

correct_rationale_plain: The region behind the spike is refractory, so current can only excite the membrane ahead, giving one-way travel.

wrong.B: Potassium channels are present throughout the axon
wrong.C: The membrane is not structurally polarized along its length
wrong.D: Myelin insulates internodes but does not enforce direction

mn: The spike cannot go back where it came from.

stem: A drug hyperpolarizes the resting potential to -90 mV without blocking any channel. What is its likely action?

options.C: It increases potassium conductance or opens potassium channels

explanation: Hyperpolarization toward the potassium equilibrium potential means the membrane has become more permeable to potassium. Opening potassium channels or increasing potassium leak conductance pulls the resting potential negative. Sodium channel opening, pump inhibition or high extracellular potassium would all depolarize instead.

Less potassium conductance or more sodium conductance means depolarization

fm.formula: resting potential follows the permeability-weighted equilibrium potentials
fm.variables: Increasing potassium permeability moves Vm toward the potassium equilibrium potential near -90 mV
fm.substitution: not needed; the direction is set by permeability
fm.why: A larger potassium conductance gives potassium more weight in setting the membrane potential

correct_rationale_plain: The membrane potential moved toward the potassium equilibrium potential, so potassium conductance increased.

wrong.A: Sodium channel opening depolarizes the membrane
wrong.B: Pump inhibition causes slow depolarization as gradients run down
wrong.D: Higher extracellular potassium depolarizes by reducing the potassium gradient

passage_text: Giant axons were voltage-clamped and their action potentials recorded at 20 °C in artificial seawater. Peak depolarization and conduction velocity were measured before and after adding channel blockers or changing extracellular potassium. Table 1 reports the resting potential, the peak of the action potential and the conduction velocity. Tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, and lidocaine is a use-dependent sodium channel blocker.
table_data:
| Condition | Resting potential (mV) | Peak (mV) | Velocity (m/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | -70 | +35 | 50 |
| TTX 1 µM | -70 | -68 | 0 |
| Lidocaine 0.5 mM | -70 | +5 | 8 |
| High potassium, 10 mM | -55 | +20 | 25 |
| TEA 10 mM | -70 | +45 | 20 |
| Ouabain 1 µM | -68 | +30 | 40 |
stem: How much does the membrane potential change during the upstroke of a normal action potential in Table 1?
explanation: The upstroke runs from the resting potential of -70 mV to a peak of +35 mV, a change of 105 mV. The amplitude is the difference between those two values, not the peak alone. This large swing reflects the change in membrane permeability from potassium-dominated to sodium-dominated.
memorize: Action potential amplitude equals peak minus resting potential
Peak is not the same as amplitude

fm.variables: Peak and resting potentials in mV
fm.why: The change in potential is the difference between the two states, and subtracting a negative adds
fm.no_calc: From -70 up to +35 crosses 70 plus 35, or 105 mV

correct_rationale_plain: The membrane rises from -70 mV to +35 mV, a change of 105 mV.

wrong.A: 35 mV is the peak value, not the change
wrong.B: 70 mV is the distance from rest to zero, ignoring the overshoot
wrong.D: 140 mV would double the actual swing

sc: Peak minus rest; subtracting a negative adds.

stem: Which pair correctly matches a channel to the phase it controls?

options.D: Voltage-gated sodium channels, depolarizing upstroke; voltage-gated potassium channels, repolarization

explanation: Sodium channels open in response to depolarization and carry the inward current of the upstroke. Potassium channels open more slowly and carry the outward current that repolarizes the membrane and ends the spike. Leak channels set the resting potential, while calcium entry triggers transmitter release at terminals.
memorize: Upstroke: voltage-gated sodium channels
Repolarization: voltage-gated potassium channels

fm.formula: upstroke from sodium influx; repolarization from potassium efflux
fm.variables: Channel opening kinetics differ: sodium opens fast, potassium slower
fm.values: not needed; phase assignment is standard
fm.why: The delayed opening of potassium channels lets the sodium-driven upstroke finish before outward current takes over

correct_rationale_plain: Sodium channels drive the depolarizing upstroke and potassium channels drive repolarization.

wrong.A: Sodium channels drive depolarization, not repolarization
wrong.B: Potassium channels drive repolarization, not the upstroke
wrong.C: Leak channels set the resting potential; calcium entry triggers release

mn: Sodium spikes it, potassium spikes it out.

stem: Which observation would best show that conduction velocity depends on axon diameter rather than on myelin?

options.A: Compare two unmyelinated axons of different diameters and measure velocity
options.B: Compare a myelinated and an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter
options.C: Block sodium channels and measure velocity
options.D: Change extracellular potassium and measure the resting potential

explanation: To isolate diameter, myelin must be absent in both conditions and only diameter varied. Velocity rises with diameter because internal resistance falls, allowing current to spread farther. Comparing myelinated with unmyelinated axons varies myelin, not diameter.
memorize: Isolate one variable at a time
Conduction velocity rises with axon diameter in unmyelinated fibers

fm.formula: velocity rises with the square root of diameter in unmyelinated axons
fm.variables: Internal axial resistance falls as diameter increases
fm.values: not needed; the comparison is controlled
fm.why: A wider axon has lower internal resistance, so local current spreads farther and faster
fm.no_calc: Same myelin status, different diameter: that isolates diameter

correct_rationale_plain: Varying diameter while keeping both axons unmyelinated isolates diameter as the cause of the velocity difference.

wrong.B: That comparison varies myelin, not diameter
wrong.C: Blocking channels changes excitability rather than testing diameter
wrong.D: Potassium changes resting potential and does not address diameter
